title: Model routing and cascades
summary: A router picks a model per request, and a cascade tries a cheap model first and escalates on low confidence or a failed check. Both save cost only if you evaluate them against single-model baselines.
useIf: Traffic mixes easy and hard requests and one model is either too costly or too weak for all of it.
avoidIf: Traffic is uniform, volume is low, or you have no eval set. A single model also gives the best prompt-cache reuse.

explain.md: Routing comes in four forms. **Rules** use task type or input length. A **learned router** is a classifier that predicts which model will do. An **LLM router** asks a small model to choose. A **cascade** runs a cheap model first and escalates when a validator fails or confidence is low. A managed option is the **Azure model router**, a deployable model that picks from a pool per request [[r16]].

explain.title: A confidence-based cascade
explain.alt: A request goes to a small model. If the output is valid and confident it is returned, otherwise the request goes to a large model whose answer is returned.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  Q[Request] --> S[Small model]
  S --> V{Valid and confident}
  V -->|Yes| A[Answer]
  V -->|No| L[Large model]
  L --> A

explain.caption: Azure model router facts (check date 2026-10-13)
head: Topic
Detail
rows: `2025-11-18` is active and updated in place. `2025-08-07` and `2025-05-19` are frozen
Balanced (default, cheapest model within about 1% to 2% of top quality), Cost (about 5% to 6%), Quality. Microsoft gives the bands as examples
Model subset limits the pool and needs at least two models for failover. Failover is on by default
Global Standard and Data Zone Standard only
OpenAI (including `gpt-6-astra`), Anthropic, xAI, DeepSeek, Meta and Fireworks models. Claude models must be deployed separately first
Effective context window is the smallest in the pool. Prompt caching helps only when the same model serves consecutive requests. Session affinity for Chat Completions is Preview

explain.md: A cascade you build yourself needs an **escalation signal**: a schema or rule check, a logprob threshold on a label (see the logprobs topic), a verifier model or agreement across samples. You must evaluate it, because the router itself can be wrong in two ways: it sends hard requests to the small model, or it escalates easy ones and wastes money.

explain.title: Evaluate a router like a model
explain.md: Replay the same traffic through always-small, always-large and the router. Report quality at equal cost (or cost at equal quality), escalation rate, router errors by segment, p95 latency including escalations, and cache hit rate. A router that wins on average can lose on one customer segment.

whereToUse: Support and chat traffic where most questions are simple and a few are hard
Extraction pipelines with a validator that can reject a weak answer
Platforms that front several teams and want one cost-controlled endpoint
Failover across models in a pool when one is rate limited
Interview answers about cost control without lowering the quality ceiling

use: Difficulty varies widely and you can measure it
A cheap check can catch a bad answer
Volume is high enough that the cost gap matters
You accept a managed router's pool and deployment limits
avoid: Long-context requests through a pool that includes smaller windows
Cache-heavy workloads where model switching breaks prefix reuse
flips: You need regional or provisioned deployments: the Azure router does not fit, so use rules or your own cascade
Prompt-cache savings exceed routing savings: pin one model
Requests exceed the smallest window in the pool: restrict the subset or route by length

pitfalls.symptom: Large requests fail only through the router
pitfalls.cause: The effective window is the smallest model in the pool
pitfalls.fix: Use a model subset with large-window models, or route long inputs by rule

pitfalls.symptom: Cache hit rate and savings drop after adopting a router
pitfalls.cause: Prompt caching helps only when the same model serves consecutive requests
pitfalls.fix: Use session affinity where available (Chat Completions, Preview) or pin one model for cache-heavy flows

pitfalls.symptom: Behaviour changes without a deployment change
pitfalls.cause: Version `2025-11-18` is updated in place and the pool can change
pitfalls.fix: Pin a subset, monitor quality continuously and re-run evals on a schedule

pitfalls.symptom: Costs rise after adding a cascade
pitfalls.cause: Too many requests escalate, paying for both models
pitfalls.fix: Tune the threshold on labelled data and track the escalation rate

scenarios.title: Mixed traffic with a managed option available
scenarios.situation: A support assistant sees mostly simple questions and a tail of hard ones. The team runs on Azure with a Global Standard deployment and wants low operational overhead.
constraints: Quality must stay within about 2% of the large model
unknowns: Which models may be in the pool?
scenarios.question: What do you adopt?

options.name: Send everything to the large model
options.why: It meets quality but pays the top price for easy traffic.
options.tradeoff: Right for low volume, or when nothing meets the quality bar.

options.name: Build your own cascade with validators
options.why: Full control over thresholds and models.
options.tradeoff: More engineering, and you evaluate and maintain the router.

options.name: Azure model router in Balanced mode with a model subset limited to models that pass your evals, then compare it with the large-only baseline
options.why: Balanced picks the cheapest model within about 1% to 2% of top quality and adds failover, with little ops work [[r16]].
options.tradeoff: The pool can change in place, prompt-cache reuse drops and the window is the smallest in the pool.

flips.if: Traffic is dominated by repeated long prefixes
flips.then: Pin one model to protect caching.
The router is unavailable, so use a cascade.

scenarios.takeaway: A managed router trades control for low operations, so measure it against baselines.

scenarios.title: Regional deployment required
scenarios.situation: A regulated team must run on regional Standard deployments in one country. Traffic has a clear easy and hard split, and a schema check catches weak answers.
unknowns: Escalation rate at the chosen threshold
scenarios.question: How do you route?

options.name: Own two-tier cascade: small model first, escalate when the schema check fails, evaluated against a large-only baseline
options.why: The managed router is limited to Global Standard and Data Zone Standard, while a cascade runs on any deployment and has a clear escalation signal.
options.tradeoff: You build, tune and monitor it, and escalated requests pay both models.

options.name: A single mid-size model for all traffic
options.tradeoff: Overpays for easy traffic or underperforms on hard traffic.

options.name: Azure model router
options.why: It supports only Global Standard and Data Zone Standard deployments.
options.tradeoff: It suits teams that can use those deployment types.

flips.if: Data zone residency satisfies the regulation
flips.then: The managed router becomes an option.
Add a logprob or verifier signal before escalating.

scenarios.takeaway: Residency can rule out managed routing, and a cascade is the portable fallback.

scenarios.title: Occasional 600,000 token requests
scenarios.situation: Most requests are short, but about 2% carry 600,000 tokens of documents. The router pool includes models with 400,000 token windows.
unknowns: Can long requests be routed by length before the router?
scenarios.question: How do you keep long requests working?

options.name: Let the router decide with no restrictions
options.why: The effective window is the smallest in the pool, so large calls can fail when a small-window model is picked.
options.tradeoff: Fine when every request fits the smallest window.

options.name: Restrict the model subset to large-window models, or route long inputs by rule to a pinned large-window model
options.why: It guarantees a model that can take the input, and short traffic keeps the cheaper path.
options.tradeoff: Long requests pay a higher price, and the subset reduces routing options.

options.name: Truncate every input to fit the smallest window

scenarios.takeaway: Check the smallest window in the pool before you route long inputs.

quiz.q: Which are true about the Azure model router?
options: The effective window is the smallest in the pool
It works on regional Standard deployments
Prompt caching helps only when the same model serves consecutive requests
Claude models must be deployed separately before they can be in the pool
quiz.explain: The window is the smallest in the pool, caching needs the same model and Claude models need a separate deployment. The router supports only Global Standard and Data Zone Standard.

quiz.q: What is the strongest evidence that a cascade saves money without hurting quality?
options: A replay of the same traffic shows equal quality at lower cost against always-large
The router has a high escalation rate
quiz.explain: Only a same-traffic comparison with baselines shows quality at cost. A high escalation rate can increase cost, and price alone says nothing about quality.

quiz.q: Match each Azure router mode to its description.

pairs.r: Cheapest model within about 1% to 2% of top quality
Limits the pool, at least two models for failover

quiz.explain: Microsoft gives the quality bands as examples. A subset restricts the pool, and failover needs at least two models in it.

flashcards.back: Rules, a learned router, an LLM router and a cascade. Azure also offers a managed model router.

flashcards.front: Which deployments support the Azure model router?
flashcards.back: Global Standard and Data Zone Standard only.

flashcards.front: How do you evaluate a router?
flashcards.back: Replay the same traffic through always-small, always-large and the router, then compare quality at cost, escalation rate, router errors by segment, p95 latency and cache hit rate.
